question.prompt: Rachel and Robert run on a circular track. Rachel runs counterclockwise and completes a lap every \(90\) seconds, and Robert runs clockwise and completes a lap every \(80\) seconds. Both start from the start line at the same time. At some random time between \(10\) minutes and \(11\) minutes after they begin to run, a photographer standing inside the track takes a picture that shows one-fourth of the track, centered on the starting line. What is the probability that both Rachel and Robert are in the picture?

solutions.explanation:
Use the standard interpretation that the photograph time is uniformly distributed between \(10\) and \(11\) minutes. In seconds, the sampling interval is \([600,660]\). Both runners must be visible at the same time, so we find the overlap of their visibility intervals.

The photographed quarter of the track extends one-eighth of a lap to each side of the starting line. A runner with lap time \(T\) is therefore visible from \(T/8\) seconds before each starting-line crossing until \(T/8\) seconds afterward. The opposite running directions do not change these intervals because the photographed arc is centered on the starting line.

Rachel crosses the starting line at multiples of \(90\) seconds. Only her crossing at \(630\) seconds has a visibility interval meeting \([600,660]\). Since \(90/8=11.25\), her interval is
\[
[618.75,641.25].
\]
Robert crosses at multiples of \(80\) seconds. Only his crossing at \(640\) seconds contributes. Since \(80/8=10\), his interval is
\[
[630,650].
\]
Their overlap is \([630,641.25]\), of length \(11.25\) seconds. Consequently,
\[
P=\frac{11.25}{660-600}=\boxed{\frac{3}{16}}.
\]
Including or excluding individual boundary times does not change this probability. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Find when both runners are visible
Convert lap times and intersect visibility intervals
